newsitem.title: ROMANIA: International analysts welcome IMF Romania move.
newsitem.headline: International analysts welcome IMF Romania move.

text.p: Analysts on Wednesday welcomed the International Monetary Fund's approval of new credits for Romania, saying it would open the door for fresh investment to underpin its reform programme.

The analysts said the decision by the Fund's Executive Board to extend $430 million in loans over 13 months was the keystone for the new government's moves to enliven Romanian markets and generate Western interest.
Other measures include passage of an austerity budget, a law allowing foreigners to own land, proposed legislation on repatriating profits and the broadening of securities markets.
"It's a key event. It highlights all the progress the country has made recently," Eric Fine of Morgan Stanley, speaking by telephone from London, said of the IMF move.

"When the portfolio repatriation rules become clearer, this will be the next key event both for people looking at the local T-bill market and the external market. Romania's local debt market will be the hottest in eastern Europe outside Russia."
New rules to change the framework of Romanian primary and secondary government securities markets and make them more active were announced this month.
Banks and financial institutions will be licensed as primary dealers if they meet certain criteria and rules governing foreign portfolio activities are soon to be debated.
Authorities are also planning fresh Eurobond issues. The first raising this year, denominated in marks, would be issued soon through Deutsche Morgan Grenfell and CS First Boston.

Analysts have become increasingly optimistic in the six months since the centrists took office after defeating ex-communists who had run Romania since the 1989 overthrow of communist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu.
Overspending by the previous leftist government put public finances deep into debt and, combined with restrictions on foreign exchange markets, prompted the IMF to halt credits.
Analysts said the latest measures would divert investors' attention away from other more developed ex-communist states, where prospects appeared to have dimmed in recent years.
"It's all very positive and will certainly encourage people to go back into Romania," one dealer said from London.
"People were already looking again at Russia, Bulgaria and Romania. Foreign investors will put Romania at the top of those countries now."

Another analyst welcomed the news as positive for Romania's international image. There was "a strong appetite" for fresh Eurobond issues, she said. "There is also great interest for the domestic markets despite unclear regulations for non-resident access to that market."
